headline: Walkable streets help people stay healthy

sources.title: Built to Move: The Benefits of Walkable Communities (NIH News in Health)
Walkable, greener neighborhoods linked to better physical and mental health (Phys.org)
Walkable Neighborhoods Can Boost Physical Activity (Washington State University)
The design of your city can help make you healthier (video, CBC News)

chunks.text: How far can you walk from your [[front door]]? In some [[neighborhoods]], people can {{get around}} on foot all day: the school, the store, and the park are just minutes away. In others, every little [[errand]] means a car trip that {{eats up}} time. This month, the National Institutes of Health {{put out}} its regular health [[newsletter]] with a big question: can the [[design]] of your street make you healthier?

verbs.correct: To move from place to place
verbs.wrong: To travel a very long way
verbs.why: Without a car, some people get around by bike and bus, and tourists often get around an old town easily on foot. In walkable neighborhoods, people can get around on foot for the school, the store, and the park.

verbs.correct: To use a lot of something
verbs.why: A long commute can eat up two hours of your day, and unexpected repairs can eat up a whole vacation budget. In some neighborhoods, even a small errand means a car trip that eats up time you could spend elsewhere.

A city sometimes puts out a report about air quality, and a school puts out a newsletter every Friday. This month, the National Institutes of Health put out its regular newsletter, asking whether street design can make you healthier.

chunks.text: The answer seems to be yes. One large study found that people who moved to more [[walkable]] cities {{ended up}} walking about 1,100 extra steps every day. Those steps {{add up}} to almost one extra hour of [[movement]] every week. Over the years, that movement helps people stay at a healthy weight and lowers the [[risk]] of [[heart disease]], [[diabetes]], high [[blood pressure]], and depression.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation
verbs.wrong: To try very hard to change
verbs.why: Skip breakfast and you end up hungry by mid morning, or take a wrong turn and end up in an unfamiliar town. People who moved to more walkable cities ended up walking about 1,100 extra steps every day.

verbs.correct: To slowly become a big total
verbs.wrong: To be too small to matter
verbs.why: Small savings can add up to real money over a year, and a few minutes of daily practice quietly add up over time. Those extra 1,100 steps add up to almost one extra hour of movement every single week.

chunks.text: Streets can change, and [[residents]] can [[lead the way]]. In one Stanford University project, neighbors {{team up}}, walk their own streets, and {{point out}} problems to local leaders: missing [[crosswalks]] or dark corners. They also {{send in}} photos to [[city planners]] through a phone app. The project has spread to more than 30 US states and 30 countries, and many [[fixes]] are cheap: paint a crosswalk, add a [[bench]], improve the [[lighting]].

verbs.correct: To join others to work together
verbs.why: Two schools might team up to clean a local beach, and police sometimes team up with shop owners to stop thieves. In one Stanford project, neighbors team up to walk their own streets and check for problems together.

A tour guide points out a castle on a hill, and a mechanic might point out a problem with your car before it gets worse. In this project, neighbors walk their streets and point out problems like missing crosswalks or dark corners to local leaders.

verbs.correct: To submit something to a group
verbs.why: Fans send in questions before a live show, and viewers sometimes send in storm photos to their local news station. Through a phone app, residents send in photos of street problems like dark corners straight to city planners.

chunks.text: You do not have to wait for your city to change. Doctors suggest small moves: park a little farther away, [[take the stairs]], or walk to the store [[instead of]] driving. Try to {{map out}} a short walking [[route]] near your home, then {{stick to}} your plan even on busy days. The [[effort]] {{pays off}} with a stronger heart and a better [[mood]].

verbs.why: A family might map out a whole road trip on the kitchen table, and a coach maps out a training plan before the season starts. Doctors suggest you map out a short walking route near your home and use it daily.

He stuck to his diet even through the holidays, and she stuck to her budget the whole time at the mall. Once you choose a walking route near your home, doctors say to stick to your plan even on busy days.

Early morning training can finally pay off on race day, and learning a second language often pays off later in many jobs. Doctors say the small effort of walking more pays off with a stronger heart and a better mood.

mainIdea.s: Streets built for walking can make people healthier. Research links walkable neighborhoods to more daily steps and a lower risk of several serious illnesses.
mainIdea.why: The article says walkable streets added about 1,100 daily steps and lowered the risk of heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, and depression.

mainIdea.s: Living on a walkable street means people no longer need any other exercise. Doctors now tell patients to skip the gym and simply stroll to the store.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the article never says walking replaces all other exercise. It says walkable streets quietly add healthy movement to normal days.

mainIdea.s: A new phone app turns walking into a points game for prizes. Players in thirty countries compete each week by choosing stairs and counting every step.
mainIdea.why: The article is about how street design shapes health, not about a step-counting game with prizes.

lines.text: [[Quick question]]: how far can you walk from your front door? School, store, park?
[[Ha]]. In my neighborhood, every errand is a car trip.

Then this is about you. A newsletter the National Institutes of Health just {{put out}} asks: can the design of your street make you healthier? In some places people {{get around}} on foot all day. In others, the car {{eats up}} all the time.
One large study found that people who moved to more walkable cities {{ended up}} walking about 1,100 extra steps a day. Those steps {{add up}} to almost an extra hour of movement a week.
An hour a week from street design alone. [[Not bad!]]
Over the years it lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, and depression.
But I can't rebuild my street.

Residents can push, though. In one Stanford project, neighbors {{team up}}, walk their own streets, and {{point out}} problems to local leaders: missing crosswalks, dark corners. They {{send in}} photos to city planners through an app.
It has spread to more than 30 states and 30 countries, and many fixes are cheap: paint a crosswalk, add a bench, fix the lighting.
Small moves. Park farther away, take the stairs, walk to the store. Doctors suggest you {{map out}} a short walking route near home and {{stick to}} it even on busy days.
A stronger heart and a better mood. [[Hard to argue with that]].
